en: Śrī.
The Great King of Tantras, Kriyoḍḍīśa, composed by the illustrious Indrajit.
[First Chapter]
Having bowed again to the bull-bannered Lord Śaṅkara, who was seated upon the peak of Ānanda together with Pārvatī, the beloved Girijā questioned him once more.
The illustrious Pārvatī said:
"O Blessed One, Lord of all gods, O Lord consisting of all knowledge! Now I desire to hear the Kriyoḍḍīśa; O All-pervading One, speak!"
Śrīśvara said:
Listen, O Goddess! I shall proclaim the supreme Uḍḍīśa Tantra;
it must be guarded with great effort, O beloved of my own life.
Having understood one's own deity, the directions, the time, and so forth, one should accomplish the six rites beginning with pacification (śānti) and their characteristics;
[these deities are] the Moon, Water, Earth, Space, Wind, and Fire.
One should accomplish the ritual action through the conjunction of their seed-syllables according to the sequence of stringing and so forth: *ṭhaṃ vaṃ laṃ haṃ yaṃ vaṃ*.
These are the respective deities.
Rati, Vāṇī, Ramā, Jyeṣṭhā, Mātaṅgī, Kulakāminī, Durgā, and Bhadrakālī— one should worship them at the beginning of any rite.
The rule regarding the seasonal periods beginning with spring.
[Thus ends the first chapter in the Kriyoḍḍīśa Mahātantrarāja, in the dialogue between the Goddess and the Lord. || 1 ||
[Now begins the second chapter:
The Armor for Liberation from All Diseases.
The Illustrious Goddess said:
O God of gods, O Great God, saluted by both gods and demons!
Now I wish to hear, O Lord, how one becomes free from disease. || 1 ||
O Supreme Lord, there is no protector for the worlds other than you;
out of supreme compassion, please tell us quickly how to ward off fever and other ailments.
The Lord said: Out of affection for you, I shall tell you of the great armor that wards off [all harm].
Oṃ! Homage to the Blessed Lady Vajraśṛṅkhalā! Strike! Devour! Eat! O you who drink blood, drink, drink!

O you who wear a garment of human bone, marrow, and blood; you whose limbs are smeared with ashes and whose body is anointed with ashes; you whose weapon is the vajra and who are encased within a vajra rampart! Release the eastern direction! Release the southern direction!

May he release the western direction; may he release the northern direction; may he bind the Lord of Wealth for the sake of the *nāgas*; may he bind the *nāga*-throne; may he bind the *yakṣas*, *rākṣasas*, and *piśācas*;
may he protect from all those afflictions such as *pretas*, *bhūtas*, *gandharvas*, and so forth; may he protect above and below.
Protect Śyenikā! Release her! Blaze, O Mahābalā! Come, come to us, Moṭi-moṭi, Saṭāvali, Vajrāgni, Vajraprākāra! Aiṃ phaṭ hrīṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ phaṭ hraṃ haṃ phuṃ pheṃ phaḥ!
From all seizing spirits, from all diseases, from all evil calamities—hrīṃ! Protect me from all [of them] without exception!
May he protect.
Thus, O Goddess, this armor is very difficult for even gods and asuras to obtain;
one should employ it against planetary fevers, spirits, and in all ritual actions.
This armor that has fallen from my mouth must not be given to just anyone;
if it were given, there would be a loss of accomplishment, and one would become a beast for the Yoginīs.
One should give it to one who is peaceful, heroic, of noble birth, and a yogi;
indeed, to one who is devoted to virtuous conduct and has completely conquered all [defilements].
Fever that lasts for one day, two days, three days, or four days— all such fevers are destroyed if one wears this armor.
It should be worn by a woman on the left hand and by a man on the right hand;
success will surely be attained—this is the truth, the absolute truth, O fair-faced one. (8)
[Thus ends the second chapter in the *Kriyoḍḍīśa-mahātantrarāja*, in the dialogue between the Goddess and the Lord. || 2 ||
[Now begins the third chapter:
The section on the worship of the earthen Śiva-liṅga for the destruction of all diseases;
hereafter, O Maheśānī, is the worship of the earthen Śiva.
Especially in the case of all diseases, there is the worship of Tryambaka.

O Goddess, having performed that by which peace shall prevail everywhere—of this there is no doubt—one should then carry out the ritual application for all [rites], such as subjugation and the rest. || 2 ||
I shall describe the ritual procedure for that; listen, O lotus-faced one.
Regarding the procedure for the worship of Śiva:
having fashioned a liṅga from clay weighing one hundred *tolakas*, and having brought and placed there the skull of a corpse, one should perform my worship. (4)
Having first established the fire, one should prepare the fourfold sacrificial site in the north,
the south, the east, and likewise in the west.
One should offer oblations with all desired objects; otherwise, it would be fruitless.

Having established a jar, one should perform my worship according to one's capacity. Then follows the installation of the fire (*vahnisthāpana*) and the installation of the severed heads (*muṇḍasthāpana*). [These consist of] three heads—of a man, a buffalo, and a cat; or alternatively, three human heads.

Having worshipped a single skull or [an image] upon it with perfumed water, having bathed it with scented water, and having crushed it upon a ground surface measuring one *vitasti*, one should construct an altar (*vedi*) over it. Right there, one should worship the Lord of Beings (*bhūtanātha*) and others in the four directions. In the east, one should worship with water for the feet (*pādya*) and other offerings, saying: "Oṃ, obeisance to the Lord of Beings."

Having performed worship, one should offer the *bali* oblation. Likewise, [one should offer it] to the Lord of the Cremation Ground in the south, to Kālabhairava in the west, and to Īśāna in the north. Having inscribed the seed-syllable of the *preta*, *hauṃ*, in the center of the altar, one should worship Bhāratī right there.
O Hero, O Corpse, O Lord of Gods, O You who have the form of a skull, O Lord of the World!
Have mercy, O Illustrious One; become the bestower of perfection upon my recitation. (6)
Having thus offered three handfuls of flowers, [one should offer] "hrīṃ namaḥ" in the southeast;
"hrīṃ caṇḍikāyai namaḥ" in the southwest; "hrīṃ bhadrakālyai namaḥ" in the northwest; and "hrīṃ dayāmayyai namaḥ" in the northeast.
May all those gods who dwell in cremation grounds and those deities who are Bhairavas show compassion; may they all grant me spiritual accomplishment. || 7 ||
With this [mantra] beginning with the *praṇava*, one should cast three handfuls of flowers;
then, touching the place [of worship], one should say, "Become submissive. (8)
Then, O Supreme Goddess, having installed the Liṅga there,
one should perform its ablution with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya), as well as with curd, milk, and other such substances.
Alternatively, O Supreme Goddess, one should perform a bath with sugar and honey mixed with the five nectars (pañcāmṛta), O Parameśvarī.
The first bath is for Īśāna, the second for Vāmadeva,
the third for Sadyojāta, and the fourth for Pinākadhṛk.

One should worship the fifth [deity], Śiva, the earthly lord of the gods of gods; now, with the root mantra and sugar, one should worship the supreme Gāyatrī. Then, having performed the jīvanyāsa, one should thereafter perform the nyāsa and other rites.
Listen to the meditation, O Mahādeva, which has been told by me out of affection. || 13 ||
I bow to Śiva, the beloved of Kailāsa, who bathes his head with the nectar-essence from two jars held in his two hands,
who holds those two deer-eyed ones [Pārvatī and Gaṇeśa] with two others, and who carries the supreme [Goddess] with two more;
he rests his two hands upon a jar of nectar placed on his lap.
I worship the three-eyed God, who wears a crown of the new moon and resides within a clear lotus. || 14 ||
Having meditated again and performed worship, thereafter one should perform the *aṅganyāsa*.
The *aṅganyāsa* is as follows:
*oṃ tatsaviturvareṇyaṃ hṛdayāya namaḥ*; *trayambakaṃ yajāmahe sugandhiṃ* [for the head].

*Puṣṭivardhanaṃ śirase svāhā* (To the head that increases nourishment, svāhā). *Bhargodevasya dhīmahi śikhāyai vaṣaṭ* (We meditate on the splendor of the Divine; to the crest-lock, vaṣaṭ). *Urvārukamiva bandhanāt kavacāya huṃ* (Like a cucumber from its stem; to the armor, huṃ). *Dhiyo yo naḥ pracodayāt netratrayāya vauṣaṭ* (May He who impels our intellects; to the three eyes, vauṣaṭ). *Mṛtyormukṣīya mā'mṛtāt astrāya phaṭ* (May I be liberated from death, not from immortality; to the weapon, phaṭ). Thus is the ritual placement upon the hands (*karanyāsa*).
Then, with the sixteen modes of worship, one should perform the worship and recitation of Aparājitā, using black bilva leaves and pippala leaves.
One should offer oblations of *karavīra* and *apāmārga* individually into the fire for Śiva one hundred and eight times each, and then perform worship.
Henceforth, O Maheśānī, honey should especially be given;
as for liquor, it should be with the juice of jaggery and ginger, but for a Brāhmaṇa [it is forbidden]. 17.
One should offer coconut water in a bronze vessel for a Kṣatriya, and for a Śūdra, one should present it mixed with honey in a copper vessel. (18)
Alternatively, O Maheśvarī, a twice-born man should offer mustard oil with clarified butter as an oblation; he should perform all the rites that have been described. (19)
O Great Goddess, listen to the mantra; it has been told to you out of faith. (20)

Oṃ. That excellent splendor of Savitṛ; we worship Tryambaka, the fragrant, the increaser of prosperity. We meditate upon the glory of the divine; may He who impels our intellects release us from bondage like a cucumber from its stem—may He deliver me from death and grant me immortality.
One should worship in various locations: in an empty house, on a riverbank, on a mountain, at a crossroads, at the root of a bilva tree, in a cremation ground, or in a secluded place. || 21 ||

O Goddess, O Śivā Tryambakā, worship [of you] brings about the pacification of all things— even for one who possesses the eight powers such as *aṇimā*, or for one who is barren, or one whose children have died, or one who is bound by royal enemies.
Therefore, O fair-faced one, I have spoken this truth, indeed the truth.
[Thus ends the third chapter in the Kriyoḍḍīśa, the great king of tantras, in the dialogue between the Goddess and the Lord. || 3 ||
[Now the Fourth Chapter: O lady of beautiful limbs, listen as I shall speak of the liberation from all diseases— the deliverance from every ailment.
One should worship eleven Rudras and offer a tenth part [of the total] with guggulu resin and clarified butter;
four water-pots, provided with five types of sprouts, should be installed.
One should worship the *liṅga* in the center of a silver eight-petaled lotus with the aforementioned mantra.
One should worship seven *liṅgas* every day after reciting [the mantra] one hundred thousand times.
Then, one should perform a fire sacrifice (*homa*) with *palāśa* wood according to that sequence, using the aforementioned mantra. (2)
At this sacred seat (pīṭha), one should consecrate the patron (yajamāna). One should give sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā) consisting of cows, land, gold, sesame seeds, and handfuls of water;
something should be given to the Brahmins, and [a specific portion] should be given to the preceptor (ācārya).
[Thus ends the fourth chapter in the Kriyoḍḍīśa, the Great King of Tantras, in the dialogue between the Goddess and the Lord. || 4 ||
[Now begins the fifth chapter:
The instruction on ritual action;
rites such as subjugation (*vaśīkaraṇa*) and others are to be performed on specific days of the week, lunar dates, constellations, and planetary configurations.
A rosary of crystal bestows all accomplishments (*siddhi*). For liberation, there are twenty-five beads; for nourishment (*puṣṭi*), twenty-seven;
with thirty, there is the accomplishment of wealth; and fifty are for the accomplishment of mantras.

With one hundred and eight [recitations], all accomplishments (*siddhi*) are attained. Medicine conjoined with the *Śiva-mantra* becomes efficacious. The ritual for uprooting and cutting medicinal herbs has been taught in the *Pūrvatantra*. It serves to eliminate defects such as sterility (*vandhyā*).
The liberation of women from afflictions: the removal of the four types of obstructive defects, such as excessive blood-flow and the like.
In this regard, the yantra consists of a triangle, a hexagon, a nonagon, and a circular mandala shape.
Having drawn these diagrams, one should cause them to be carried out preceded by mantras.
Through the worship of the tantra and the consumption of medicinal herbs and other substances, there is the pacification of defects.
[Thus ends the fifth chapter in the Kriyoḍḍīśa, the great king of tantras, in the dialogue between the Goddess and the Lord. || 5 ||
[Now begins the sixth chapter:
The Peaceful Armor for those who have lost children, etc.
Peace for those whose children have died, whose wombs are barren, or who are childless comes from wearing this armor. The Armor.

First: Oṃ, salutations to Narasiṃha; salutations to the destroyer of great calamities; salutations to Narasiṃha of divine form. Sthauṃ kṣauṃ, salutations to Rāma. Rāṃ, salutations to Rāma. Oṃ hrīṃ śrīṃ phaṇaṃ huṃ hāṃ, by the sound of the *phetkāra*, [protect] every child.
For the destruction of all fears and calamities, if one recites and maintains this vidyā, then Narasiṃha shall always protect [them]. Hūṃ Phaṭ Svāhā!
This is the second armor by another method.

Oṃ, homage to Narasiṃha, the rending of the chest of Hiraṇyakaśipu, the pervader of the three worlds, the destroyer of the hosts of bhūtas, pretas, piśācas, and ḍākinīs, arisen from a pillar! Take away, take away all defects! Poison, poison! Cook, cook! Churn, churn! Strike, strike! Phaṭ! Huṃ!

*phaṭ ṭhaḥ ṭhaḥ*, come, Rudra commands you, *svāhā*. *Oṃ kṣauṃ*, obeisance to the Blessed One Narasiṃha, who wears a garland of flames, whose fangs are blazing, whose eye is fire, the destroyer of all *rakṣasas*, the annihilator of all *bhūtas*, the destroyer of all fevers— burn!

*Daha paca paca rakṣa rakṣa hūṃ phaṭ svāhā*. Having inscribed this on birch bark with *gorocanā* and fashioned it into a pill with gold, it should be worn on the left hand by a woman or the right hand by a man; there will never be any harm.
[Thus ends the sixth chapter in the Kriyoḍḍīśa, the Great King of Tantras, in the dialogue between the Goddess and the Lord. || 6 ||
[Now begins the seventh chapter.
The Goddess said:
"I have heard the unprecedented account of the armor (kavaca), which is desired by the gods."
Now I desire to hear; O Lord, tell me of the yantra.
The Lord spoke the Yantra: "The letter 'Ra' devoid of its vowel-measure (mātrā), and likewise the head on the side."
Therefore, the six-cornered yantra, which is of the nature of illusion (māyā), becomes supreme. || 2 ||
The seed-syllable of Māyā, *hrīṃ*, is the core.

By wearing it on the left hand of a woman, a barren woman shall become possessed of sons. By placing it around the neck of a young girl or even a boy, they shall become happy. Having written it with *gorocanā* on birch bark, one should wear it encased in gold.

By writing the sixteen-spoked wheel (*ṣoḍaśīcakra*) on birch bark with *gorocanā* and wearing it, there is an increase in the good fortune of women. By drawing a four-cornered wheel and placing "hrīṃ" within it, and wearing it on the upper arm, a woman will have living sons; or else, having written the syllable *praṇava* and so forth, followed by "kṣaṃ," within the four corners, [and] the fish-wheel (*mīnacakra*).
By writing [the mantra] and wearing it, a barren woman becomes one whose children live.

Beyond this, in the center of the pericarp of an eight-petaled lotus, is the *māyā* [syllable]. Thereafter, in the middle of each petal, write two *māyā*-seeds repeatedly. After this, having written the *māyā*-seed upon a nine-petaled [lotus], [place it] on the arm.

By wearing [this amulet], a woman whose children have died gives birth to living children. Having inscribed [the mantra] with *gorocanā* and saffron, wrapped it with a red thread, and bathed the pill with the five nectars (*pañcāmṛta*) and the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*), one should consecrate it with the *praṇava* and bathe it with fragrant substances. Then, having established the vital breaths (*prāṇa*), one should contemplate it as having the form of the deity.
Having worshipped the pill, one should wear it.
For the rite of subjugation, one should bathe the image of Śiva with ghee or even with honey.
Likewise, O Goddess, with milk and other substances, one should perform it for the sake of pacification and also in the Mṛtyuñjaya rite.
For attraction, it is used with honey; for cruel rites, with ashes.
Its quantity is proclaimed to be one hundred tolas of this substance.
O Goddess of the gods, one should offer that measure of powdered consciousness as a food offering (naivedya),
and likewise present one hundred and eight bilva leaves and flowers.

For rites such as pacification (śāntika), one should use *droṇapuṣpa*; for malevolent rites (abhicāraka), *barbara*; and for paralyzing (stambhana) and deluding (mohana), *dhattūra* and the flower called *kanaka*.
O Goddess, for the purpose of inciting enmity and eradication, Vijayā and Aparājitā are [to be used],
beginning from the fourteenth day until the next fourteenth day.
One should worship each individual *liṅga* in succession with a spirit of devotion;
furthermore, one should perform the recitation (*japa*) one thousand and eight times every day.
It is taught that for seven days one should perform recitation, worship, and so forth, according to the ritual procedure of Caṇḍogra, using seven liṅgas; or else, for five days, using five.

O beloved Queen of the Gods, for rites of pacification (śāntika), the recitation and worship should be performed with the Vaṭuka mantra, or with that of Mañjughoṣa, or with the Traiyambaka mantra. (10)
One should perform recitation and worship according to the specific ritual procedures for each occasion,
whether it be during the destruction of one's caste, the extinction of one's lineage, or in times of danger from disease such as fever.
When great fear has arisen and when all manner of malevolent spells occur,
O Goddess, one should diligently worship one hundred and eight lingas.
O Goddess, at the beginning of the Atirudra-yoga or otherwise, one should propitiate Śiva with the Rudrādhyāya or with the Nīlakaṇṭha-stava.
I pay homage to you, O Lord of Beings; protect me, O Sovereign of the World!
Save me from sins and from hells, O you who are affectionate toward your devotees.
O Lord, O Mahādeva, O Sovereign of the Thirty-three Gods, protect me from birth, death, old age, disease, desire, anger, greed, and delusion. (7)
You are my refuge, you are my intellect, you are my ground, and you are my ultimate resort;
may my devotion to you be firm through body, mind, and speech. (8)
This is the declaration of the fruit: this Rudra-kavaca destroys sin through its recitation;
it was proclaimed by Bhairava through the grace of Mahādeva. (9)
No sin remains in his bodies, nor does any fear exist for him;
he attains happiness, health, sons, and an increase in longevity. || 10 ||
One desiring a son obtains sons; one desiring wealth shall obtain wealth;
one desiring knowledge obtains knowledge; and one desiring liberation attains liberation itself.
One afflicted by disease is freed from illness, and one who is bound is released from bondage;
even sins such as the killing of a Brahmin perish merely by reciting this.
[Thus ends the eighth chapter in the Kriyoḍḍīśa, the Great King of Tantras, in the dialogue between the Goddess and the Lord. || 8 ||
[Now begins the ninth chapter:
One seat is declared to be Siddhāsana, and the second is Kamalāsana.
All accomplishments are attained on a tiger skin; the accomplishment of knowledge is attained on a deer skin.
A seat made of cloth removes disease; one made of cane increases affection;
that of silk is said to bestow nourishment; and a woolen blanket grants all perfections.
Whether it be white or black, especially a red woolen blanket; for the purpose of subjugation one should use a seat of sheepskin, and for attraction, a tiger skin.
For pacification, the skin of a deer is recommended; for the sake of liberation, the skin of a tiger;
for immobilization, O Goddess, the skin of a cow; and likewise, the skin of a horse for driving away.
In rites of inciting hatred, one should employ a dog’s hide; for killing, one should perform the rite prescribed with a buffalo’s hide.
Likewise, O Goddess, a seat of silk cloth bestows all desired objects.
A seat of kusha grass or a woolen blanket is honored for all ritual acts;
however, a seat made of wood or stone destroys suffering and poverty.
One should perform the daily and occasional rites by installing the sacrificial vessel (homaghaṭa) and other items, or one may perform them upon a sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila);
this should be made very beautiful with sand, measuring one cubit in size.
O Supreme Goddess, one should place five jars filled with water;
they should be established with two mantras and accompanied by sprouts.
And if one is unable, O Great Goddess, with even a single garment; or at some time, O Śivā, one should cover all the food with just one.
Having placed [the vessel] so that its water is uncovered, one descends.

Then, having stabilized the jar with the mantra "sthāṃ sthīṃ śrīṃ," one performs the sprinkling of the jar with "klīṃ," the consecration of the jar with "krāṃ," and the installation with "hrīṃ" using water.
Filling [the vessel]. Then, with palms joined in reverence, one should recite:
"May all rivers beginning with the Gaṅgā, as well as the oceans and lakes," || 10 ||

May all the oceans, rivers, lakes, clouds, and streams; the holy ponds, springs, and those situated in heaven, the netherworld, and on earth; and all sacred pilgrimage sites, take up their residence within this jar. (11)
Then, with the root mantra, one should sprinkle the sprout with "Śrīṃ," the fruit with "Hūṃ," the vermilion with "Raṃ," and the flower with "Baṃ";
the *dūrvā* grass with "Oṃ Oṃ Oṃ" for sprinkling; and strike with *kuśa* grass using "Oṃ Phaṭ Svāhā. For the sake of pacification, one should bathe the jar.
Having caused the proclamation of an auspicious day (*puṇyāha*), one should perform the ritual acts beginning with the binding of the directions (*digbandhana*).

One should worship Gaṇeśa, the planets, the guardians of the directions (*dikpāla*), and so forth, at each sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*). On the sacrificial mound (*sthaṇḍila*), one should worship the Liṅga which destroys all calamities; one should also worship it in the water-pot (*kumbha*). Then, having brought the fire and consecrated it—

One should perform the fire sacrifice (*homa*). In times of great calamity, one should offer oblations of *javā*, black *parājitā*, *droṇa*, or *karavīra*; thus one shall obtain the fruit desired by the mind.
An oblation performed with white and red *karavīra* flowers mixed with red sandalwood,
along with *droṇa* and *ketakī* flowers, shall liberate one from disease.
With *campaka* flowers, white lotuses, red lotuses (*kokanada*), and *bandhūka*;
with *bilva* leaves, *kuruvaka*, *munipuṣpa*, and *kesara*. (14)
O Great Goddess, if one performs the oblation, one will certainly possess a son;
[one should offer] a red lotus, a bilva leaf, gold, and something of red color. 15.
O Maheśānī, one should also offer oblations with the three pacifying mantras in the sequence of a hundred; then all accomplishments will arise.
[Thus ends the ninth chapter in the Kriyoḍḍīśa, the great king of tantras, in the dialogue between the Goddess and the Lord. || 9 ||
[Now begins the tenth chapter:
The Śākta Consecration.
The Śākta consecration brings about peace for those who are barren, those whose children die in infancy, and those afflicted by disease.

This consecration (abhiṣeka) increases wealth, fame, and longevity; it generates good fortune, fulfills all hopes, wards off defects in mantras, removes malevolent spells (abhicāra), destroys the afflictions of the planets, bestows all spiritual accomplishments (siddhis),
and delights the eyes.
Having prepared a lamp, one should then drop soot into a copper vessel;
having stirred it with cow’s ghee, one should then apply it to the eyes.
Then, one sees exactly what was seen previously. || 1 ||
O beautiful one, when combined with red sandalwood and honey in water,
even a small amount of this collyrium, when applied, destroys cataracts.
Furthermore, another [remedy], Punarnavā-ghṛta, immediately produces the brilliance of vision. || 3 ||
The root of the *apāmārga* plant, when tied with a thread spun by a maiden, removes fever;
likewise, under the asterisms of Svāti and Vaiṣṇava (Śravaṇā), it destroys even the most severe fever.
To ward off all fevers,
one should cause the root of red *vāṭyā* to be placed on the bed with banana fibers on a Sunday; this removes all fevers, including those caused by heat.
For the pacification of abdominal diseases,
drinking the root of Nageśvara with honey brings relief from abdominal ailments and destroys thirst.
Having sprinkled red sandalwood and taken one *tolaka* mixed with water in the left hand,
one should recite the mantra one hundred and eight times and drink it; within seven days, his thirst will be destroyed.
O auspicious one, the mantra consists of two seed-syllables of sound; one should utter the word "nāśaya" twice,
then pronounce the word "tṛṣṇoti," and finally "svāhā"— this is considered the mantra.
By this mantra, O Goddess, the destruction of craving will come to pass. || 5 ||

Now, O Maheśānī, I shall describe the great auspicious rite (*mahāsvastyayana*) which pacifies all calamities; listen to this great auspicious rite, which brings about all accomplishments, is meritorious, and destroys all sins. (6)
It pacifies all calamities, destroys all portents of death,
alleviates great diseases, and eradicates epilepsy.
Yoginīs, bhūtas, vetālas, pretas, kūṣmāṇḍas, and pannagas— especially the ḍākinīs and others— do not remain in that place.
O Goddess, one should worship Kṛtyā according to the prescribed rule, preceded by [the preliminary rites].
One should draw a sixteen-spoked lotus together with a pair of yonis and a bindu.
Having drawn an eight-petalled lotus in the center of that, one should place the letters beginning with *ya* in sequence;
and in the center of that, one should draw a hexagon while recollecting the root mantra.
One should draw the lunar disc in the center; for one who is otherwise unassailable, [one should draw] Śiva along with the earthly [disc].
In its center, one should place a water-pot adorned with a garland of flowers around its neck.
In its center, one should place Kṛtyā, endowed with all auspicious marks;
one should worship her according to the prescribed ritual order and offer the *pāyasa* (milk-rice) oblation. || 12 ||
Having gratified [the deities] and placed the Bhairavas, such as Asitāṅga and others, within the jar,
one should worship them with perfumes, flowers, and so forth, and outside of that, the guardians of the field (kṣetrapālakas).
O Goddess, one should worship the World-Protector (Lokapāla) and perform a fire-oblation (homa) before him;

Meditating upon the goddess Kālikā, who shines with the splendor of mantras, moral conduct, and patience; who is as blue as the sky, the Great Fierce One, the crusher of gods and demons.
