With "īśānena vandanām" [one performs] salutation. Again, the root mantra: *Oṃ īśānaḥ sarvavidyānām īśvaraḥ sarvabhūtānāṃ brahmaṇo'dhipatir brahmā śivo me 'stu sadāśiva oṃ*. Śiva.

I pay homage; salutations! Then follows the consecration of the vital breaths (*prāṇapratiṣṭhā*): Āṃ Drīṃ Kroṃ Haṃsaḥ. Salutations to Vaṭuka Paśupati, the wielder of the trident. May the vital breaths (*prāṇāḥ*) come here; may the life-force (*jīva*) remain here. May all the senses—the eyes, ears, nose, and breath—come here and abide happily for a long time.

Svāhā! Having veiled [the deity] with "Hūṃ," having rendered [it] nectar with the "Vaṃ" syllable and the *dhenumudrā*, and having performed the binding of the directions with finger-snaps (*choṭikā*), one should worship the six limbs and then worship the Deity. Reciting the root mantra: "This is the water for the feet (*pādya*). Oṃ, to Mahādeva, whose form is the Moon, who is the soul of the *baṭuka*."

Salutation to Paśupati, to Śiva. In this manner, one should offer the arghya, ācamanīya, and other items in sequence. Regarding the bath (snāna), however, there is a specific procedure as follows: "Today," and so forth, [for the sake of] such-and-such person, preceded by the removal of all inauspiciousness, for the pacification of planetary portents and misfortunes, and for health and long life—

With the desire for prosperity, I bathe the Liṅga of Paśupati in the form of Vaṭuka with one hundred *tolakas* of milk. One should bathe it while reciting "Oṃ, I take refuge in Sadyojāta," and so forth. Then, having bathed it with water, [one applies] the root mantra. Likewise for the fragrance: "Oṃ, salutation to Mahādeva, whose form is the Moon. For the flowers:

Now, with the words "Today," and so forth, as previously stated, one should offer one hundred and eight *droṇa* flowers to Śiva, the Lord of Beings (*paśupati*) in the form of a *baṭuka*, out of desire [for liberation]. Reciting the root mantra and the mantra:
*oṃ mahādevāya somamūrtaye namaḥ*, one should offer them one by one. Thus...

Bilva leaves; honey-mixture (*madhuparka*); incense and lamps with fragrance; and the food offering (*naivedya*). "Today," and so forth, as in the ritual for the bathing materials, with such-and-such a desire: "I offer this food offering of one hundred *tolakas* of sun-dried rice, together with its accompanying implements, to you, Śiva, the Lord of Creatures in the form of Baṭuka. *Oṃ*, to Mahādeva.

Salutation to Soma-mūrti. One should offer a powder of one hundred *tolakas* of *saṃvid*, as well as water and betel-leaf, having made the formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*) as before. Reciting the root mantra for the rite of subjugation (*vaśīkaraṇa*), [one should say]: "Oṃ, to Bhava, the Water-form, the self of Vaṭuka, to Śiva."

*Namaḥ*. One should worship in this sequence. In this manner, one should offer the *arghya* and *ācamanīya*. For the bath, however, reciting the root mantra, one should say: "Today, for the sake of subjugating [the name] so-and-so, I bathe the *pāśupata-śivaliṅga* in the form of Baṭuka with one hundred *tolakas* of ghee mixed with honey. In this way...

For the incense: *Oṃ bhavāya jalamūrtaye*. For the flowers: "Today [and so forth], for the purpose of subjugating such-and-such a person, I offer one hundred and eight *droṇa* flowers to Baṭukātman Paśupati Śiva. Reciting the root mantra: "This *droṇa* flower, *Oṃ bhavāya*..."

"Salutation to Jalamūrti"—thus for each [deity]. Likewise for the *bilva* leaf. For the incense and lamp, however: "Oṃ, salutation to Bhava, Jalamūrti. As for the food offering (*naivedya*), however: "Today, etc., for the purpose of subjugating such-and-such a person, I offer this food offering consisting of one hundred *tolakas* along with its accessories, Oṃ, to Śiva, who is Paśupati in the form of Vaṭuka."

I have offered. Having recited the root mantra: "This food offering, weighing one hundred *tolakas*, together with its accessories, and the *saṃvidā* powder, [I offer] to Oṃ Bhava, the embodiment of water, obeisance. Then, one should give water for drinking, water for sipping (*ācamanīya*), and betel leaf.

Then one should worship the eight enclosures (*aṣṭāvaraṇa*). Then one should worship the eight forms (*aṣṭamūrti*). Then, having offered three handfuls of flowers with the root mantra (*mūla-mantra*) and made the formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*), one should recite that mantra one thousand times, whether for rites of pacification (*śāntika*) and so forth, or even for fierce rites (*krūra-karman*). Then, having completed the recitation with the "Secret" (*guhya*) and other [mantras], one should perform the hymn of praise (*stotra*) and so forth.
One should recite [the mantra].
Then follows the offering of the *bali*: as follows—having uttered the root mantra: "This *bali* is offered with homage to Baṭukabhairava!
Together with the hosts of Bhairava’s retinue, drink, drink my enemies along with their blood; [consume] this *bali*!"
Seize, seize! Svāhā! Oṃ! Day by day, consume the blood and the flesh of the enemy faction, together with your own retinue and accompanied by dogs! 50.

Then, one should perform the fire-oblation (*homa*) one hundred and eight or one thousand times with the prescribed substances. For subjugation (*vaśīkaraṇa*), however, there is a fire-oblation of one thousand and eight mustard seeds smeared with ghee. For the purpose of pacification (*śānti*), [one uses] *dūrvā* grass and so forth; for cruel rites (*krūrakarman*), bilva leaves; and for eradication (*uccāṭana*), [the mantra is]: *oṃ hrīṃ huṃ śivāya*.

*svāhā*. This is the specific [mantra]. [I offer] the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) to you, Śiva, the Lord of Beings (*paśupati*), in the form of the *baṭuka*: "I give this to you. White mustard seeds and salt.
[Thus ends the thirteenth chapter in the *Kriyoḍḍīśa*, the Great King of Tantras, in the dialogue between Umā and Maheśvara.]
[Now begins the fourteenth chapter:
The Armor of the Six Rituals that Crushes Enemies.
The Illustrious Goddess said:
I have heard the greatness of Vaṭuka, which causes complete wonder;
now I desire to hear the armor (kavaca) of the six ritual acts.
Śrīśvara said:
Listen, O Goddess, I shall declare that which you ask of me;
by either hearing it or reciting it, there is the destruction of enemies at that very moment.
The Goddess said:
"Reveal to me the armor for the purpose of enchanting the three worlds—that which is capable of destroying and annihilating the enemy of the three worlds. (3)
Thus addressed, Mahādeva, the Lord of the World, becoming enraged,
awakened the Goddess with words that rained down nectar.
The illustrious Mahādeva said:
O Great Goddess, you who are supremely devoted, from where does this thought arise in you?
The Illustrious Goddess said:
"One may strike back against one who seeks to kill; by that, one does not become a slayer of a Brahmin.
There is an ancient Vedic scripture stating: 'In whatever way people approach me...'"
O Lord, if you indeed have compassion for me, please tell me [the means] for the eradication and subjugation of enemies, for the purpose of destroying their lives. (7)
For men are always striving for the purpose of destroying their strength. || 8 ||
The Lord said: Listen, O Goddess, O highly fortunate one, O beloved of the vital breath of the fire of time!
By the mere retention of which, the destruction of enemies shall occur. (9)
Having seized him by the base of his foot and touched him, he treated him like a slave;
yet, one who has merely sought refuge cannot be destroyed. || 10 ||
Listen, O illustrious goddess! Comprehend this with full attention:
when enraged, he is Time itself for the purpose of destroying the lives of enemies. (11)
Ten-faced, ten-armed, ten-footed, with the luster of collyrium, Kālī, possessing the radiance of ten million suns, destroy my enemies!
Having destroyed them, O Goddess, in an instant, destroy all other enemies as well. 12.

Kṛṃ kṛṃ kṛṃ! O Ugraprabhā (of fierce radiance), O Vikaṭadaṃṣṭrā (of formidable fangs)! Delude, delude the opposing faction; cook, cook; churn, churn; burn, burn; strike, strike; kill, kill those who are intent on harming me! Ward them off, ward them off with the circles of Yoginīs; cut, cut; pierce, pierce, O Karālinī!
Seize, seize! Oṃ krīṃ krīṃ krīṃ krīṃ! Flash, flash! Fill, fill! Purify, purify! Cull, cull! Strike, strike! Blow, blow! Slay, slay! Bring all the world under control! Oṃ namaḥ svāhā!
Thus, O Goddess, has this armor been proclaimed by Bhadrakālī;
if one should wear it written on birch bark or placed within gold, [it will grant protection]. 13.
If one wears it on the crest-lock, the right arm, or the neck, it shall,
through its wrath, delude the three worlds and pulverize the three worlds in an instant.
He shall possess sons, wealth, and wisdom, becoming a treasury of various sciences;
furthermore, by the mere touch of his body, weapons such as the Brahmāstra and others [shall become effective]. (15)
Enemies meet their destruction when [the enemy's name] is smeared with silver;
within a single month, it becomes the cause of great calamity for those enemies. (16)
Whatever enemy a mortal remembers while reciting this armor-armor (kavaca), he certainly destroys that very person instantly; I tell you this as a truth. (17)
If one maintains [the practice], the enemy will suffer constant parching of the throat;
trembling of the heart arises as long as his compassion does not intervene. (18)
The Lord spoke the Mohanaka armor: "O Goddess, that which was concealed during the three periods of time has now been revealed in the Kali age."
It should not be spoken, nor should it be seen; yet, out of affection for you, it is being revealed.
O Goddess Kālī, naked one, who causes the enchantment of the world!
Listen to that, O Great Goddess; this is the enchantment of the three worlds. (20)
The seer (ṛṣi) of this [mantra] is Mahākālabhairava, the meter (chandaḥ) is Anuṣṭubh, the deity (devatā) is Śmaśānakālikā, and its application (viniyoga) is for the purpose of enchanting all.
Aiṃ Krīṃ Krūṃ Kraḥ Svāhā! May she always protect me in dispute.
Klīṃ! To the deity Dakṣiṇakālikā, who bestows victory in the midst of the assembly. 21.
Kṛṃ kṛṃ! O you with the dark-blue body, kill, kill the enemy!
Hrīṃ kṛṃ kṛṃ klīṃ! Bring the three worlds under your control! || 22 ||
Hrīṃ śrīṃ krīṃ! Protect me, protect me in disputes and in the presence of kings.
O twenty-two-syllable Brahman, always protect me everywhere. (23)
Wherever the armor is excluded, may the Kīlakas protect me there;
O Goddess Śyāmā, who possesses a fierce form, protect me everywhere. (24)
The supreme delusion of these [beings] has been revealed through your good fortune;
whoever shall always recite this will bring the three worlds under their control. (25)
If one should worship the goddess of terrible form without knowing this armor-mantra, he will always be afflicted by great diseases; of this there is no doubt. (26)
O Nārada, it has been told to you that such a person shall be short-lived and afflicted by disease;
however, this is especially so unless one wears this armor (kavaca) inscribed upon birch bark.
Having donned the armor along with the yantra, the accomplishment of one's desires arises.
On the eighth day of the bright fortnight, one should write the mantra and wear it upon a golden leaf.
O great sage, I am unable to describe the majesty of this armor;
a yogi seeking its fruit should wear it on his topknot or on his right arm. (29)
O Goddess, this Kalpadruma is being revealed out of affection for you;
it should be concealed with effort and recited, O great sage.

Aiṃ Krīṃ Krūṃ Kraḥ Svāhā! May she always protect me in dispute. Klīṃ! To the deity Dakṣiṇakālikā, who bestows victory in the midst of the assembly; Krīṃ Krīṃ! To the dark-limbed one, slay the enemy, slay him! Hrīṃ Krīṃ Klīṃ! Bring the three worlds under my control! Hrīṃ Śrīṃ Krīṃ! Protect me!
"Protect me in disputes, in the king's domain; O Brahman of twenty-two syllables, protect me always everywhere!
Śrī Viṣṇu said:
"O Mahālakṣmī, let this armor (kavaca) be recited thus constantly."
The three worlds, including all that is moving and unmoving, will certainly come under one's control. || 31 ||
This was previously told by Śiva to Nārada, the source of strife;
by its recitation, even the world of moving and non-moving beings was deluded by Nārada.
[Thus ends the fourteenth chapter in the Kriyoḍḍīśa, the great king of tantras, in the dialogue between the Goddess and the Lord. || 14 ||
[Now begins the fifteenth chapter:
The Armor that Provides All Protection;
the Illustrious Goddess said:
O Blessed One, Lord of the gods of gods, worshipped by all the Vedas; O God, you have told me everything, yet the armor (kavaca) has not been revealed.
If you have affection for me now, O Lord, reveal to me the armor (kavaca) of the mantra known as Prāsāda, which brings about all forms of protection.
The Blessed Lord said:
For the armor-mantra (kavaca) of the temple (prāsāda), Vāmadeva is the seer (ṛṣi), Paṅkti is the meter (chandas), and Sadāśiva is the deity (devatā);
its application (viniyoga) is proclaimed for the attainment of the practitioner’s desired goal.
May Sadāśiva, known as Prāsāda, always protect my head;
and may Maheśvara, whose nature is the six-syllabled mantra, protect my face. (3)
May the Blessed One, whose self consists of five syllables, protect my two arms;
may Mṛtyuñjaya, whose self consists of three seed-syllables, always protect my life.
May the imperishable Dakṣiṇāmūrti, seated at the foot of the banyan tree and assuming the form of the thirty-six syllables, protect me always from all sides. (5)
May Rudra, whose essence consists of twenty-two syllables, protect my belly;
may Nīlakaṇṭha, whose essence consists of three syllables, always protect my throat.
May Hara, the Lord of all women, who is the wish-fulfilling gem in the form of the seed-syllable and the bestower of all prosperity, always protect my secret organ. (7)
May Maheśvara, whose nature is the single syllable, who is the embodiment of the peak-syllable (kūṭa), and who is Mārtaṇḍabhairava, eternally protect my feet. 8.
May the destroyer of Tripura, whose nature is the great seed-syllable "Oṃ," the lord of the thirty gods, always protect me on the field of battle.
May Īśāna protect me always above, with his head held high;
may Tatpuruṣa, the leader of the mountains, guard me in the southern direction.
May Mahādeva, known as Aghora, protect me in the east;
may Vāmadeva always protect me in the west;
and may Sadyojāta, who bears his own essential form, always protect me in the north.
O Goddess, he who recites this armor-mantra (*kavaca*), which provides protection and is difficult even for the gods to obtain, at the time of dawn, shall attain his desired fruit. (12)
The practitioner who recites this on his right arm at the time of worship will bring gods, humans, and gandharvas under his control; of this there is no doubt. (13)
O Goddess of gods, if a man wears this armor upon his head, the eight supernatural powers, beginning with *aṇimā*, are as if held in his hand.
The wise man, having placed this vidyā upon a golden leaf wrapped in a white cloth and set within a silver interior, should wear it. 15.
Having attained great fortune and the mantra, one who bears the form of Śiva must never give it to just anyone, nor should it ever be disclosed.
One should reveal it to a disciple who is endowed with devotion and is a practitioner;
otherwise, there will be a loss of accomplishment. This is the truth, O beautiful one. (17)
Out of affection for you, O Great Goddess, this auspicious armor has been told. It must not be given to anyone, O Blessed One, if one desires one's own welfare. (18)
O Great Goddess, whoever worships with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings this armor (kavaca) spoken from my own mouth, by him all the gods are worshipped; of this there is no doubt. (19)
[Thus ends the fifteenth chapter in the Kriyoḍḍīśa, the Great King of Tantras, in the dialogue between the Goddess and the Lord. || 15 ||
[Now the sixteenth chapter: The Tryambaka-Mṛtyuñjaya Mantra; the Illustrious Goddess said:
Now I wish to hear about the Tryambaka [mantra] previously mentioned;
O Lord, please explain its classification and the *mṛtasañjīvanī* rite of pacification.
Īśvara said: Listen, O Goddess, I shall explain that which you ask me of:
why, O Mother, Hara was born from the womb of three Mothers. || 2 ||
Therefore, O Maheśvarī, my name is declared as Tryambaka;
Vasiṣṭha is said to be its seer (ṛṣi), and the Anuṣṭubh is cited as its meter (chandas). || 3 ||
The deity intended for this [rite] is the Three-Eyed Lord of Pārvatī;
and by means of the distributed syllables of the mantra, one should perform the visualization of the six limbs (ṣaḍaṅga).
Then, one should visualize a rampart all around with a stream of water from the fire-seed syllable (vahnibīja),
and thereafter perform the formal resolve (saṅkalpa).
O Queen of the Gods, having again performed the mental resolve (saṃkalpa) and the purification of the elements (bhūtaśuddhi) and so forth,
you should thereafter perform the ritual placement on the hands (karanyāsa) for me, O beautiful one.
To Tryambaka, salutation with the two thumbs; we worship him with the two index fingers, svāhā;
the fragrant one who increases prosperity with the two middle fingers, vauṣaṭ;
like a cucumber from its stem with the two ring fingers, huṃ; may I be released from death with the two little fingers, vauṣaṭ.
*Phaṭ* from *māmṛtāt* with both palms and backs of the hands. Likewise in the heart and other [limbs].
Then one should place the twenty-two syllables of the mantra on the eastern, western, southern, and northern faces (4);
on the chest, throat, and upper face (3); again on the navel, heart, back, and belly (4); and on the genitals, anus, thighs, and the end of the feet (6).

One should place the syllables of the mantra in sequence: on the two knees (2), on the two ankles (2), on the two breasts (2), on the two sides (2), on the two feet (2), on the two hands (2), on the two nostrils (2), and on the head (1). Then, one should again place them in the eleven locations beginning with the feet: on the head (1), on the pair of eyebrows (1), on the eyes (1), and on the mouth (1).

One should perform the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) as follows: on the two cheeks (1), the two arms (2), the heart (1), the abdomen (1), and again on the genitals (1), the thighs (1), the knees (1), and the feet (1).
Then, having meditated according to the described visualization and worshipped with mental offerings, [one should present] the special water for honor (*viśeṣārghya*).

Having established the worship, invocation, and other rites as prescribed by Śiva, and having offered five handfuls of flowers, one should worship Varuṇa. One should worship the six limbs with "Tryambakam hṛdayāya namaḥ" and so forth.
Then, on the eight petals, [one should worship]: *oṃ arkāya namaḥ*; likewise for Indu, Vasudhā, Jala, Vahni, and Vāyu.

In the sky for the sacrificer, outside of that, starting from the east: *oṃ rāmāyai namaḥ*, *oṃ rākāyai namaḥ*, *oṃ prabhāyai namaḥ*, *oṃ jyotsnāyai namaḥ*, *oṃ pūrṇāyai namaḥ*, *oṃ uṣase namaḥ*, *oṃ pūṣāyai namaḥ*, *oṃ svadhāyai namaḥ*, *oṃ viśvāyai namaḥ*, *oṃ vidyāyai*.
Homage! Oṃ, homage to Sitā; oṃ, homage to Kṛti; oṃ, homage to Śraddhā; oṃ, homage to Sarā; oṃ, homage to Sandhyā;
oṃ, homage to Divā; oṃ, homage to Niśā. Outside of that, oṃ, homage to Āryā; oṃ, homage to Ārdrā; oṃ, homage to Prajñā; oṃ, homage to Medhā.

Oṃ, salutation to Kānti (Beauty). Oṃ, salutation to Śānti (Peace). Oṃ, salutation to Puṣṭi (Nourishment). Oṃ, salutation to Buddhi (Intellect). Oṃ, salutation to Dhṛti (Fortitude). Oṃ, salutation to Mati (Mindfulness). Then one should complete the ritual from the offering of incense (dhūpa) up to the final dismissal (visarjana).
As for the practical application: during the transit of Saturn or Mars, one should touch the root of an Aśvattha tree and recite [the mantra] one thousand times.
O Maheśvarī, by performing everything according to the rules for *puraścaraṇa*, one shall be liberated from death itself; what need is there to mention other trivial rites?
Every day, the practitioner of mantra should perform oblations according to the rite for the four sacrificial mounds,
using two thousand blades each of *dūrvā*, *vaṭa*, *javā*, and *karavīra* flowers.
One should offer oblations of bilva leaves, palāśa, and likewise kṛṣṇāparājitā,
as well as fuel-sticks of the vaṭa tree, up to ten thousand times.
There shall be an abundance of wealth and grain; this is the truth, the absolute truth, O Maheśvarī! || 10 ||
O Goddess, listen hereafter to the *mṛtasañjīvinī* mantra. First is the seed-syllable of the temple (*prāsādabīja*), followed by the death-removing *tāraka*, and then the *vyāhṛti*.
Having recited Tryambaka, he who constantly mutters it in the form of a *saṃpuṭa* and in direct order; || 11 ||
Through the recitation of the *mṛtyuñjaya* mantra beginning with "tryambakam," all perfections (*siddhi*) are attained.
One should recite this mantra; one will certainly be swiftly liberated from disease. (12)
Hauṃ (—) Oṃ Jūṃ Saḥ (—) Oṃ (—) Bhūr Bhuvaḥ Svaḥ.
Listen to the meditation, O Great Goddess:
a pure, clear lotus is situated [in the heart], and two full jars are placed upon both hands.
May the Lord— who holds in his two lotus-hands a rosary and a water-pot eternally full,
who pours from those two [vessels] upon his head, and whose crescent moon bathes his body with nectar— grant us the pure glory that destroys the web of worldly existence. 13.
Having meditated thus, [one should say] "Salutation to Tryambaka, the Great Rudra.
If that [rite] is extremely formidable, then one should worship the Supreme Lord.
Then follows the *sādhana* of the Yoginīs beginning with "Surasundarī" and so forth; then the *sādhana* of the Bhūtinīs.
Regarding the *sādhana* of the Bhūtinīs, the Śrīdevī said:
The *yoginīsādhana* has been understood as the supreme *bhūtinīsādhana*;
tell me that, O Mahādeva, if you have compassion for me. (15)
Śrīśvara said: The first is the goddess Vibhūṣiṇī, followed by Parā, Kuṇḍaladhāriṇī,
Hāriṇī, Siṃhinī, Haṃsinī, and then Naṭī.
Kāmeśvarī is likewise proclaimed, and then her beloved Ratidevī;
thus the eight heroines have been described, who bring happiness to practitioners. (17)
O Great Goddess, the sādhana of Ādyāvibhūṣiṇī is according to her mantra; thus is Ādyāvibhūṣiṇī and her mantra.
HŪṂ PHAṬ PHAṬ HRĪṂ BHŪTINĪṂ HŪṂ HŪṂ HŪṂ;
the two wrathful weapons at the end of the *māyā*, and BHŪTINĪṂ from the three *kūrca*s. (18)

Alternatively, listen, O Goddess of Gods: Oṃ hrīṃ hrīṃ phaṭ phaṭ vibhūṣiṇī hūṃ hūṃ hūṃ. [This consists of] Tāra (Oṃ), two instances of Lajjā (hrīṃ), two instances of Astra (phaṭ), Vibhūṣiṇī, and two instances of Krodha (hūṃ). This is the visualization.
She holds a small knife in her right lotus-hand and a slender sword in the other;
her chest is graced by towering breasts and adorned with swaying necklaces and ornaments,
yet her body is smeared with the flesh, blood, and fat from between her teeth.
May she, dark as the color of a black cloud and encircled by serpents, protect us. || 19 ||
There, at the foot of a tree, for three days during the night,
he should recite the mantra eight thousand times while meditating with a one-pointed mind.
At the conclusion of the recitation, one should perform a great worship and offer incense once again;
by offering the arghya mixed with sandalwood water, [the deity] will certainly be pleased. (21)
Whether as a mother, a sister, or a wife, she becomes joyful and gratified;
having made the three worlds as clear as a myrobalan fruit held in the palm of her hand, she becomes his mother.
If the illustrious sister [is present], he gives the collyrium-ornament to one who has a retinue of one hundred and eight, even from a distance of a thousand yojanas.
Having brought a woman, he gives her divine elixir and rejuvenating medicine;
if she becomes his wife, he ascends upon her back and goes eternally to heaven.
The Goddess, the ever-adorned one, fulfills all hopes with a thousand dīnāras, as well as mercury and the elixir of immortality (rasāyana). 25.
O Goddess, O Maheśvarī, hear now the practice of the supreme Kuṇḍalinī and the meditation upon the supreme Kuṇḍalinī:
she who wears earrings in her ears, whose face is like the moon, who is playful and smiling.

May she who wears earrings—the source of a mass of bliss for the three worlds—protect us; her waistband hangs upon the slope of her mountain-like hips, she has bewildered the three worlds, and her high, jar-like breasts shine with the luster of rays from her pearl necklace. 26.
One should worship her in a cremation ground and perform ten thousand recitations;
then the goddess, wearing earrings, arrives at that very moment.
The practitioner should also offer red arghya; when she is satisfied, she says:
"What should be done by me, O child? and the practitioner says, "O Mother. (28)
And give fifty dīnāras, O Giver of the Three Worlds!
Now follows the sādhana of Sindūrahāriṇī, O fair-limbed one; this is the mantra of Sindūrahāriṇī. (29)

Joined with the two *krodhas* and the moon (*indu*), followed by the word "sindūrahāriṇī," and the three *kūrca* seed-syllables, as well as the weapon (*astra*)—thus is the various [mantra] proclaimed. (30)

Her form is captivating like the hue of vermilion; her voice resonates from branches swaying with trembling leaves; her slender body is made beautiful by longing; and her smile is like the white-rayed moon.

May she protect us— she who possesses a pair of creeper-like arms raised high, darkened by the continuous luster of her teeth within, yet bringing beauty to the three worlds, and captivating with her vermilion mark.

Having gone to a deserted temple at night in a secluded place, the practitioner should perform the recitation of one thousand repetitions of the *tattva* [mantra] for as many days as there are *tattvas*. (32)
At its conclusion, the excellent practitioner should perform a grand worship with garments, ornaments, and decorations; then his desired wife shall become his.
"Choose a boon quickly! Thus addressed, Sindūrahāriṇī said:
"O Goddess, Sindūrahāriṇī protects for twelve days. (34)
O Goddess, hear now from here on the great mantra of Siṃhinī, the sādhana of Siṃhinī:
two *māyās*, two *krodhas*, and then the word "Siṃhinī. (35)
Again, at the end of that is Krodha, and then Siṃhinī, the great mantra: Hrīṃ Hrīṃ Phaṭ Phaṭ Siṃhinī Hūṃ Hūṃ Phaṭ. || 36 ||
Likewise, the worship of Siṃhinī should be performed on a mountain peak or in a secluded place.

Meditation is a fortress difficult to traverse like the peaks of mountains; the Daityas are like dense forests, yet she who has fallen from the lioness’s womb perceives the entire universe resting upon the tip of a single hair on Viṣṇu’s foot.

May that digit protect all that remains, which— by the force of her army of elephants and her staff of power— has caused the Siddha women to flee in haste, while she herself appears like the terrifying dissolution of the entire race of Death.
While she stood upon the peaks of mountains, amidst trees, in rugged fortresses, and within the depths of inaccessible caves inhabited by Daityas—
her feet treading upon the entire universe as it was cast down from her hair, her moon-throne fallen away,
and the forest-dwelling Siddha women agitated as they grasped the stars for lamps— she remained there.
May she, whose mass of hair is filled with a garland hanging down over all the heads [of the gods], protect this entire world.
Having gone to Ekaliṅga at night, one should mutter the mantra ten thousand times;
then, being worshipped, Siṃhinī becomes delighted and grants excellent boons.

"What shall I do?"— thus speaks his wife when she is desired. At the end of the day, during the night, she comes as a lioness and gives to the practitioner a pair of garments filled with nectar day after day.
O lady of beautiful limbs, listen hereafter to the procedure for the *sādhana* of Haṃsinī. Oṃ hūṃ hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ, Haṃsinī!
The mantra described as the *haṃsinī* consists of the *praṇava*, the three *kūrca*s, and the weapon (*astra*). || 41 ||
She is Meditation (Dhyānā),
whose eyes resemble a white and a non-white lotus; she is endowed with a pair of arrows,
attended with respect by the devoted wife of a simple man from a noble family who desires to hear her.
May the divine Śrīhaṃsinī protect us—she whose face is slightly turned with sidelong glances, tremulous and charmingly smiling, and who is graced by divine golden necklaces and jewels. || 42 ||
Vajrapāṇi, having gone to his home, should draw a beautiful image;
having worshipped it with focused attention, he should recite the mantra ten thousand times.
Until midnight, the goddess Haṃsinī certainly arrives;
by offering sandalwood and the arghya libation, Haṃsinī is seen.
"O practitioner! Tell me quickly what I should do for you;
I shall provide garments, ornaments, and food as divine offerings. (45)
Because there is no remaining expenditure, he does not give and becomes angry. || 46 ||
The Sadhana of Naṭī:
Hereafter, O Mahāmāyā, hear from me the sadhana of Naṭī.
Oṃ hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ phaṭ naṭī hūṃ hūṃ hūṃ. || 47 ||
One should extract the syllable *tāram* (OM), followed by the two *kūrca-krodha-astra* mantras (*HŪM PHAṬ*), and then the word *naṭī*.
This mantra, consisting of three *kūrca*s (*HŪM HŪM HŪM*), is declared to be the mantra of Nartakī.
Dhyāna has a face as beautiful as the interior of a full-blown blue lotus, with high, pitcher-like breasts;
she shines with eyes like a pair of deer or fish, and possesses a joyful, gentle smile.
Born from the ocean of milk, radiant, the destroyer of the enemies of her devotees, distinguished by her mastery of lute and song, the Blessed One is the eloquence of speech. 49.
Having gone to the dwelling of a low-caste woman (nīcapāśa) and performing recitation and worship for seven days, the Naṭī becomes well-accomplished; one should offer incense repeatedly.
One should offer an oblation of sandalwood and a delightful food offering;
such a dancer becomes a wife who always grants the enjoyment of all desires.
Having abandoned expenditure, one obtains a single golden fruit;
day by day, the goddess Naṭī certainly becomes stable. (52)
O Great Goddess, hereafter listen to the accomplishment of the maidservant, the summoning of the maidservant. || 53 ||

The mantra consists of the Tāra (Oṃ), followed by two Kūrca syllables (Hūṃ Hūṃ), and after that, a pair of Astra syllables (Phaṭ Phaṭ); then the two Ceṭīs and the two Krodhas are declared— this is the most excellent of all Ceṭī mantras.
Oṃ hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ phaṭ ceṭī hūṃ hūṃ! This goddess, who speaks of nectar, has a moon-like face and her upper garment has slipped down.
Carrying a golden jar and a stainless lotus at her parting,

her pure body adorned with sandalwood paste and other unguents, honored by her fragrance, and her voice as sweet as that of a female ruddy goose slightly subdued by the heat— may that handmaid Prabhā protect you. 55.
Even here in this terrifying place, by the mere utterance of her name,
a female servant surely approaches and performs the work of a servant.
Alternatively, one should perform the recitation for three nights at the door of one's own house;
then the Goddess will surely come and perform the work of a servant.
The Sadhana of Kameshvari; the ritual application of Kameshvari:
first the Tara (Om), then the Kūrca (Hrīm) and the Astra (Phaṭ) twice, followed by Kameshvari Bhūtinī.
The mantra of Kāmeśvarī is said to consist of the three Krodhas ending with "paraṃ ṅentaṃ. || 58 ||
In meditation:
Oṃ! She is joined with the palm-tree trunk, possessing sweetness and endowed with flowers;
she is Gāyatrī, with sweet lips, a smiling face, and holding a lute as she sings.

May this Kāmeśvarī Bhūtinī—whose eyes are like red lotuses, who is endowed with the intoxication of honey-wine, who wields the flower-bow, and whose face is as sweet as nectar—protect us from every side. 59.
Having gone to that place and partaken of meat, and having offered an oblation (bali) consisting of meat and other substances, one should perform a thousand recitations (japa). || 60 ||
Having recited the Manumarka mantra one thousand times, one shall attain perfection;
when the recitation reaches midnight, one should present an offering (arghya) with blood. || 61 ||
Kāmeśvarī shall become pleased; she becomes the desired wife and certainly fulfills all hopes, bestowing a kingdom with certainty. 62.
The *kumārīsādhana* is:
*hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ phaṭ devyai hūṃ hūṃ hūṃ*. One should extract the two wrathful syllables, the pair of *astras*, and the word "devī."
The three secret Krodhas and the supreme Kumārī-mantra are the innermost secret.
When accomplished, she becomes a wife of divine form— a maiden with the golden luster of a celestial bow, adorned with every ornament, and endowed with meditative concentration.
Having gone to a temple at night, one should prepare a bed there;
one should offer white cloth, sandalwood, and jyotiḥpuṣpa flowers.
Having offered incense of guggulu resin, one should recite the mantra eight thousand times;
at the conclusion of the recitation, she always arrives, engaging in kissing, embracing, and other such acts.
The maiden goddess Satyā becomes his beloved wife;
she bestows eight dīnāras as well as a pair of divine garments. (67)
He will provide divine, desirable food for his retinue;
having quickly brought goods from the houses of other hermitages, he bestows them.
Having recited [the mantra] a thousand times daily, that maiden indeed comes;
this is the truth, the truth, and again the truth—listen to me, O beloved of my life! (69)
Repeatedly reciting the mantra of Krodha, the supreme mantra,
[he meditated on] the Lord of Wrath, whose face is the sky, who holds a vajra in his hand, and who is the destroyer of the gods.
Whoever recites this mantra with a desire for accomplishment without understanding it, his ritual action will be fruitless and he shall eventually fall into hell.
Prosperity is called *bhūtinī*, and accomplishment is called *siddhi*; she is the creeper upon the wish-fulfilling tree of the Kali age. (71)
O Goddess, listen now to the supreme means for achieving the perfection of Sundarī, which is the sequence of practice for the sādhana of Sundarī.
O Śivā, one should worship each [of these] individually according to the divisions beginning with Sundarī.
Having risen early in the morning and bathed well, one should perform the daily rites;
then, having ascended the temple, one should go to the most beautiful place of worship.
At the root of a bilva tree, in a cremation ground, in a wilderness, or at a crossroads—staying there, the yogi should accomplish the practice of the yoginīs and the bhūtinīs. 74.
Seated upon a deer-skin, pure, he should apply a tilaka mark on his forehead;
then, having performed the ritual sipping of water (ācamana) according to the rules, he should offer the arghya oblation to the Sun.
Having performed the recitation for auspiciousness and the chanting of peace-mantras again and again,
one should worship Gaṇeśa and Baṭuka upon the yantra.
Then, having turned toward the north, one should perform the formal resolve (saṃkalpa) there;
O Supreme Goddess, one should worship Gaṇeśa and Krodhabhairava.
One should perform breath control (prāṇāyāma) with the root mantra and carry out the six-limbed ritual placement (ṣaḍaṅganyāsa).
Then, having meditated once more as before, one should worship with mental offerings.

Having prepared the *arghya* and performed the installation there, one should draw an eight-petalled lotus on a cloth; and having fashioned a seat in its center, one should smear it with sandalwood paste. (79)
One should write the seed-syllable of Lañjā there, and having meditated upon it again, one should worship it;
one should worship the Hero at night, and worship the Paśu during the day.
O Mahādeva, the wise one should recite the root mantra continuously for a month;
then, at midnight, having performed worship and an offering according to the rules,
he should recite the mantra fearlessly and offer it within his heart.
O Great Goddess! Hereafter follows the supreme sādhana of the yakṣas;
the mantra of the yakṣa.
He is the sky, the grasper, and indeed the one whose crest-jewel is the joined half-moon. || 82 ||
If this great one-syllable mantra is recited by practitioners eight thousand times, it bestows all accomplishments. (83)
The Goddess said:
"O Moon-crested Lord, I have heard the great mantras of the yakṣas beginning with Bhīmavaktra; O Master, tell me their meditation (dhyāna) in brief."
The meditations of the yakṣas consist of the Bhīmavaktra meditation:
[the deity] stands in the pratyālīḍha posture, is black, and has short, variegated hair.
Two-armed, holding a flaying knife in her right hand and a skull-cup in her left, she wears a tiger-skin garment, has three eyes, and a terrifying face. (85)

One should meditate upon the deity Mahāvaktra through the Mahāvaktra-dhyāna: the god Mahāvaktra is fire-colored, three-eyed, and two-armed; he holds a sword in his right hand and a shield in his left hand.
With black, curly hair, a distorted face, and terrifying in appearance, he grants fearlessness and boons to the practitioner. (87)
One should meditate upon the god with the face of a lion; he is endowed with a mass of matted hair, has a distorted countenance, two tongues, four eyes, and two ears. (88)
He has two arms; in his right hand he holds a mace, and in his left he displays the gesture of fearlessness.
Hayānana is white; he has a horse's face, is entirely two-armed, and is extremely terrifying.
He holds a hand-drum (ḍamaruka) in his right hand and a trident (triśūla) in his left. (90)
One should meditate upon the god Mahāvīra with the meditation of Mahāvīra: he has two ears and three eyes, two arms, a smiling face, and bestows boons and fearlessness. || 91 ||
[Thus ends the sixteenth chapter in the Kriyoḍḍīśa, the Great King of Tantras, in the dialogue between Gaurī and Īśvara. || 16 ||
[Now begins the seventeenth chapter:
The Ritual for Mṛtyuñjaya.
The Illustrious Goddess said:
O Lord of my life, ocean of compassion, expert in the scriptures, tell me:
what is the fruit of the worship of Mṛtyuñjaya, and what is its ritual procedure?
The illustrious Śiva said:
"O Gaurī, out of affection for you, I am not able to refuse to speak;
yet, the ritual procedure for Mṛtyuñjaya must not be disclosed to one who is turned away from the truth."
But, O Goddess, beloved of my life, this must be spoken with effort in the mouth:
"Mahādeva, the Conqueror of Death, is the supreme, manifest remover of death. (3)
O beautiful one, listen as I describe his ritual procedure in brief;
O Goddess of gods, how the method of worship for the sake of pacifying disease is performed. (4)
Having fully worshipped the Mṛtyuñjaya Liṅga, the Lord of the Three Worlds,
one afflicted by disease is freed from disease, and one who is bound is released from bondage.
But he who worships with devotion the Liṅga presided over by Mṛtyuñjaya—even Yama would bow down with devotion; what then could a commoner do?
I shall describe the procedure for its worship; listen, O beloved of my life!
Having taken eighty *tolakas* of clay according to the distinctions of caste...
Having fashioned an earthen linga,
the wise man should place it upon a radiant base and perform recitation with the Puranic mantra.
The wise one should bathe [the image] with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya), eight *tolakas* for each; he should bathe it with each individual substance while reciting its respective mantra.
Desiring the destruction of disease, the learned Brahmin, having sat upon a seat and put on a washed garment, should [proceed] preceded by the mention of his name, lineage, and so forth.
Having indeed worn a rosary of rudrākṣa beads around the neck and the triple mark of sacred ash, one should diligently offer the sixteen modes of worship with devotion. (11)
A golden seat should be given, as well as ornaments;
one should also present a pair of garments that may be worn. (12)
Having fashioned a six-cornered mandala as the Śiva-yantra, one should write the name of the person to be accomplished (sādhya) at its center,
and then write the Prāsāda-bīja, "Hauṃ," within the six corners.

Having written the syllables of the five-syllabled mantra together with the *praṇava* and the six-limbed mantras (*ṣaḍaṅgamantra*), and having fashioned five petals outside of that, [one should assign] on those petals: *oṃ īśānāya namaḥ*, *oṃ tatpuruṣāya namaḥ*, *oṃ aghorāya namaḥ*, *oṃ sadyojātāya namaḥ*, and *oṃ vāmadevāya namaḥ*.

One should write the five mantras in the sequence starting from the east. Having fashioned eight petals outside of that, one should write the letters of the Mātṛkā on those petals. Outside of that, one should encircle it with the *tryambaka* mantra.
Having worshipped this yantra through recitation (*japa*), fire-oblation (*homa*), and other rites, one should wear it. The attainment of longevity, health, sovereignty, and so forth will occur.
Now listen, O Goddess of gods, to the Mṛtyuñjaya Yantra, or rather, the Yantra that bestows all perfections. (13)

In the center, one should inscribe the *dhruva* (the syllable *oṃ*) enriched with the syllables of the target; on the cardinal petals, the middle [syllable] of the mantra; and in the corners, the final [syllable] of that mantra. That yantra, consisting of the earth-element (*kṣiti-bhuvana*), with the moon in the cardinal directions and the letter *ḍha* in the intermediate directions, is said to remove all fears, poison, spirits, and untimely death.
It is joyful, as it pacifies the suffering of disease and delusion; it is the seat of glory and bestows renown. || 14 ||
One should offer the madhuparka in a bronze vessel along with a pair of meals,
and one should present a thousand unbroken bilva leaves.
Having thus worshipped a single liṅga, one should mutter the mantra two thousand times;
there, one should perform a fire sacrifice (homa) with guḍūcī fuel-sticks.

O Goddess, one should give a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) to the Brāhmaṇa consisting of gold and clothing, or half of that, or half of that again, according to one's wealth and with due respect. || 17 ||
One who is deficient in limbs should not perform worship, for it yields no fruit;
by propitiating even a single linga, one obtains the same fruit that would be gained in another age.
O Goddess, in the Kali age, one obtains that fruit multiplied fourfold; having placed eighty tolas of water in a vessel made of mango wood, [one attains this merit]. (19)
O Goddess of the gods, having cleansed the sick person with that very water using [the appropriate] *kulas*,
one should cast [the essence] into the flame of a lamp while reciting the *mānaka* mantra.
In this manner, according to the prescribed injunctions, one should worship my linga;
whatever kind of disease there may be, it shall go to destruction—this I have declared.
Having performed the worship with all its constituent parts, one obtains the desired fruit;
however, through the omission of any part, the mental impression becomes in vain.
The sick person is instantly liberated, like a serpent casting off its slough;
if there is devotion to my word, then one will certainly be liberated. (23)
Otherwise, O Goddess of the Gods, everything becomes fruitless. (24)

O Goddess, listen hereafter to the procedure for the worship of the yantra, the ritual method for worshipping the yantra. O Goddess, having performed the daily obligatory rites and preceded by the recitation of auspicious benedictions, [one should proceed].
And then he should perform the formal resolve (saṃkalpa) in accordance with the words of the ritual injunctions.

"Today," and so forth: "I, [Name], of such-and-such lineage, the venerable Devaśarman, for the sake of worshipping the deity presiding over this yantra, shall perform the consecration of the such-and-such mantra.
Having thus made the formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*), O Great Goddess, one should perform the worship of the Guru.
Then, having prepared the five products of the cow (pañcagavya), it should be consecrated with the Śiva-mantra.
There, the mantra-practitioner should cast the wheel, thoroughly permeated by the syllable Om;
then, having lifted that wheel, he should place it in a golden vessel.
With the five nectars, milk, musk, and saffron, and with milk, curd, ghee, honey, sugar, and so forth, in their respective order. (28)
One should prepare the unsurpassed five nectars (pañcāmṛta) with water and incense;
[one should worship] the Goddess with eight jars filled with water.
One should perform the supreme bath with waters enriched by decoctions;
having completed the bath, one should place that Goddess upon a golden throne.
Just as with the Gāyatrī: "We know the King of Yantras; we meditate upon the Great Mantra; may that Yantra inspire us.
Having touched the yantra with the tip of a blade of kuśa grass, one should consecrate it with the Gāyatrī mantra.
One hundred and eight times, O Goddess, for the sake of attaining the state of divinity. || 31 ||
Then, having performed the purification of oneself, one should worship the deity with the six limbs;
there, O Great Goddess, having invoked [the deity], one should perform the ritual placement of the vital breath (jīvanyāsa). || 32 ||
Regarding this Prāṇapratiṣṭhā mantra: Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśvara are the seers (ṛṣis); the Ṛg, Yajur, and Sāma Vedas are the meters (chandās);
Consciousness (caitanya) is the deity; and its application (viniyoga) is in the rite of Prāṇapratiṣṭhā.
There, one should worship Śiva with the sixteen services, as well as with the Mahāmudrā and other gestures, and with fruits, betel, and food offerings.
O Maheśvarī, one should offer silk thread and the like, as well as garments and ornaments, along with agallochum, a fly-whisk, and a bell, according to what is appropriate.
One who is intent on his own welfare should bestow all of this with diligence;
thereafter, he should recite [the mantra] one thousand times for the sake of accomplishing every desired object. (35)
One should perform the conclusion of the recitation with an eight-limbed prostration;
having offered one hundred and eight oblations, one should pour the residual clarified butter (sampāta) [into the fire].
If one is unable to perform the fire-sacrifice (homa), one should perform twice the number of recitations (japa).
One should give a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) to the preceptor, and thereafter dismiss the Goddess.
The procedure for this is as follows:

having performed the daily obligatory rites (*nityakriyā*) and preceded by the recitation of auspicious verses (*svastivācana*), one should make the formal resolve (*saṅkalpa*). "Today," and so forth, [I], of such-and-such lineage, the venerable Amukadevaśarman...

"For the purpose of worshipping such-and-such deity, I shall perform the consecration of such-and-such yantra. Then, having brought the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*), one should empower it one hundred and eight times with the mantra *Hauṃ* and cast the yantra into it while reciting the *Praṇava* (*Oṃ*). Thereafter, having lifted it out, one should bathe it with cool water, sandalwood paste, fragrant scents, and musk.

Having bathed [the deity] with saffron and brought the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*), one should consecrate it one hundred and eight times with the mantra *hauṃ*, purify it with the *praṇava* (OM), and then bathe [the deity]. The sequence there is as follows:
having first bathed [the deity] with milk, one should offer incense; likewise with curd and ghee.

With honey and sugar; then one should bathe [the deity] with eight jars. One should bathe [him] with waters mixed with saffron, gorocana, and sandalwood. In every instance, the bathing is performed with the root mantra. Then, having lifted up the yantra and touched it with the tip of a *kuśa* blade, one should consecrate it by reciting the Gāyatrī one hundred and eight times.

One should perform the *prāṇapratiṣṭhā* (consecration of the vital breaths). For this *prāṇapratiṣṭhā-mantra*, Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśvara are the seers (*ṛṣis*); the *Ṛg*, *Yajur*, and *Sāma* Vedas are the meters (*chandāṃsi*); Consciousness (*caitanya*) is the deity;
and its application (*viniyoga*) is in the consecration of the vital breaths. It is as follows: *āṃ hrīṃ krauṃ yaṃ raṃ laṃ vaṃ*.

*Śaṃ ṣaṃ saṃ hauṃ haṃsaḥ*. "The vital breaths (*prāṇāḥ*) of the deity [named] so-and-so are here as vital breaths; the life-force (*jīva*) is established here; all the sense organs, speech, mind," and so forth—having thus established the vital breaths, one should invoke the primordial deity (*prakṛtidevatā*) there and worship her with either the sixteen or the five offerings (*upacāras*). Therein:

Having offered silk thread and other such items, and having recited the mantra one hundred and eight or one thousand times, one who is able should offer a *bali* oblation. Then, one should perform one hundred and eight *homa* offerings; in the absence of *homa*, the recitation (*japa*) should be performed twice as many times.
Then, having given the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*), one should perform the rite for securing against defects (*chidrāvadhāraṇa*).
[Thus ends the seventeenth chapter in the Kriyoḍḍīśa, the great king of tantras, in the dialogue between the Goddess and the Lord. || 17 ||
[Now begins the eighteenth chapter:

First, having drawn a hexagonal maṇḍala, one should write the seed-syllable *prāsāda* (HŪM) together with the name of the person for whom the rite is intended at its center; then, one should write the letters of the five-syllabled mantra accompanied by the *praṇava* (OM) within the six corners.

In the openings, having fashioned five petals outside the six-limbed mantra, one should write the five mantras— *oṃ vāmadevāya namaḥ*, *oṃ īśānāya namaḥ*, *oṃ tatpuruṣāya namaḥ*, *oṃ aghorāya namaḥ*, and *oṃ sadyojātāya namaḥ*— on those petals in the order starting from the east.

Having fashioned eight petals outside of that, one should write the letters of the Mātṛkā on those petals. Outside of that, one should encircle it with a circle using the Tryambaka mantra. Recitation, fire-offerings, and other rites should be performed within this yantra using the Mṛtyuñjaya mantra.

In the center, one should inscribe the syllable of the person to be accomplished (sādhya) together with the *dhruva* mantra; in the middle of the cardinal petals, the syllable *anta*; in the corners, *manas*; then in the directions, the world of *takṣitibhu*; and in the intermediate directions, the syllable *candra*.
This Yantra, ending with the letter *ḍha*, is said to remove all fears, as well as poison, spirits, and untimely death.
It brings joy by pacifying the suffering of disease and delusion, bestows prosperity, and grants renown.
The ritual procedure for the *Tryambaka-mṛtasañjīvinī* for the sake of pacifying disease:
[He is] pure, seated upon a clear lotus; in both hands he holds full jars, and with two others, in his lotus-like palms, he holds two water-pots that are eternally full.
May the Lord, who bears two flowing streams from his two [eyes] upon his head and bathes his body with nectars like the crescent moon, grant you a pure splendor through a multitude of kalpas.

First, having uttered the seed-syllable of the temple (*prāsādabīja*), then the *tāraka* which removes death, and the *vyāhṛtis*, he who constantly recites the *tryambaka* mantra in its encapsulated form (*saṃpuṭa*) and in direct order (*anuloma*),
as well as the first quarter of the *gāyatrī* and then the first [quarter] of the *tryambaka* which bestows auspiciousness— [he attains the goal].
Having first performed meditation, he who recites the mantra "manavo 'tu" indeed certainly overcomes death.
The seed-syllable of the palace is *hauṃ*, which removes death; it is the three-syllabled *mṛtyuñjaya* mantra:
*oṃ jūṃ saḥ*. It is the savior (*tāraka*). Then the *vyāhṛti*: *bhūḥ bhuvaḥ svaḥ*. With that, [the sequence is] *hauṃ jūṃ saḥ*. Then *oṃ bhūḥ bhuvaḥ svaḥ*.
Thereafter, the *tryambaka* mantra is enclosed (*sampuṭita*) by the preceding mantra in the direct order (*anuloma-krama*); by the recitation (*japa*) of this—
All success is attained. Furthermore, the meditation on the first quarter of the *gāyatrī* and the first quarter of the *tryambaka* mantra, and so forth, has been previously described.
[Thus ends the eighteenth chapter in the glorious *Kriyoḍḍīśa*, the great king of tantras, in the dialogue between the Goddess and the Lord. 18
[Then the nineteenth chapter:
The Illustrious Goddess said: "O Blessed One, Lord of the Gods of gods, who are worshipped by the deities!"
O Lord, you have told me everything, yet the armor has not been revealed.
O Lord, tell me now, O Protector, if you have affection for me, that which provides protection from death and destroys all that is inauspicious.
Śrīśvara said:

Of this Mṛtyuñjaya mantra, Vāmadeva is the seer (ṛṣi), Gāyatrī is the meter (chandas), Mṛtyuñjaya is the deity (devatā), and its application (viniyoga) is in recitation for the sake of attaining the desired goal of the practitioner.
May Sadāśiva, the conqueror of death, always protect my head; and may Maheśvara, whose nature consists of the six-syllable mantra, protect my face. (3)
May the Blessed One, whose self consists of five syllables, protect my two arms;
may Mṛtyuñjaya, whose self consists of three seed-syllables, always protect my life.
May the imperishable Dakṣiṇāmūrti, seated upon a Bilva tree and assuming the form of the thirty-six phonemes, protect me always from all sides. (5)
May Rudra, consisting of twenty-two syllables, protect my belly;
may Nīlakaṇṭha, whose self consists of three letters, always protect my throat.
May Hara, the wish-fulfilling gem, who is half-woman and the bestower of all prosperity, always protect my private parts with the *bījapūra* fruit. || 7 ||
May Maheśvara, whose nature consists of the three syllables, who possesses a secret (kūṭa) form, and who is Mārtaṇḍabhairava, eternally protect my feet. 8.
Oṃ jūṃ saḥ! May Īśāna, the destroyer of Tripura whose nature is the great seed-syllables, always protect me from above on the crown of my head. 9.
May Mahādeva, the leader of the mountains, protect me in the south;
may the Great God named Aghora protect me in the east.
May Vāmadeva always protect me in the western direction;
may he who bears the form of Sadyojāta always guard me in the northern direction.
O Goddess, he who recites this protective armor (*kavaca*), so difficult even for the gods to obtain, in the presence of Śiva at dawn and at midday— 12.
By the grace of this armor, he attains his desired fruit;
indeed, the practitioner who wears this armor on his right arm [achieves success]. (13)
It bestows all accomplishments, is meritorious, and destroys all calamities;
[it subdues] yoginīs, bhūtas, vetālas, pretas, kūṣmāṇḍas, and pannagas. || 14 ||
They do not cause him harm; rather, they treat him like one who has sons. O Goddess, having recited this, one should worship according to the prescribed ritual.
A hundred thousand recitations of the root mantra are prescribed as the preliminary rite (puraścaraṇa);
by wearing it, O Great Goddess, there is the destruction of death and disease. (16)
Thus, the mortal who performs this shall attain a meritorious state;
O Great Goddess, know that this [truth] always resides within his mouth. (17)
By the grace of this armor, a man shall be freed from death;
otherwise, there will be a loss of spiritual attainment. This is the truth, O beautiful one. (18)
Out of affection for you, O Great Goddess, this auspicious armor has been told;
it must not be given to anyone, O Blessed One, if one desires one's own welfare.
[Thus ends the nineteenth chapter in the glorious Kriyoḍḍīśa, the great king of tantras, in the dialogue between the Goddess and the Lord. || 19 ||
[Now begins the twentieth chapter: The Section on Yantras; the Yantra for the Barren Woman.
Henceforth, O Goddess, listen to the supreme method of wearing the yantra;
by the mere wearing of the yantra, one shall obtain the fruit of all desires. || 1 ||
And that woman who is barren may become possessed of virtuous sons;
then she should draw this unsurpassed yantra with gorocanā and other substances. || 2 ||
Having drawn two circles, one should draw an eight-petalled lotus;
in each petal, one should write the *māyā* seed-syllable, and then [draw] the square enclosure (*bhūpura*).
O Maheśvarī, one should write this yantra on birch bark and wear it;
by wearing this great yantra upon the abdomen, a woman shall become possessed of auspicious sons.
There is no other practice [permissible] elsewhere than in a life-threatening crisis;
having given a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) to the guru, one may then receive this supreme yantra. || 5 ||
One should draw a circular four-petalled lotus provided with a perimeter of earth-walls (bhūpura); in the center of the circle, O Goddess, one should specifically write the name of the practitioner.
One should write the word *putravatī* first, followed by the word *bhavatu*;
then, the syllable of modesty (*lajjā*) enclosed by three *praṇavas* should be written three times upon the petals.
O Goddess, one should worship as before and wear it on the right arm;
truly, truly, O Queen of Gods, even a barren woman shall become possessed of sons.
If a woman be unfortunate, she shall become fortunate within a month. || 9 ||
Henceforth, I shall proclaim the protective yantra, which is the supreme provider of great protection;
by its wearing, even the lord of the Dānavas becomes a great protector.
O Goddess, one should draw a five-petaled lotus marked with the seed-syllable *glauṃ*;
having written the five *gaṃ*s in the very center, if one should wear it, [it brings success]. || 11 ||
He shall have no fear for his son; there, Hara is the protector.
One should write [the mantra] on birch bark with *gorocanā* and saffron and wear it.
In that regard, O Great Goddess, Gaṇapati should perform the worship;
when worshipped and worn, it indeed destroys all calamities. (13)
One should again draw an eight-petaled lotus within the lotuses;
having drawn it with yellow orpiment, O Supreme Goddess, one should wear it.
O Maheśvarī, for one who performs the worship of the *liṅga* in the manner described and wears it, there shall indeed be the destruction of untimely death. 15.
Having drawn a circle with a central dot as a "son-producing" yantra, one should then draw an eight-petalled lotus;
thereafter, one should write the seed-syllable *yaṃ* individually upon each petal.
O Goddess, one should worship as before; through this concentration (dhāraṇā), death is destroyed, and it is the supreme means for a woman who has borne only one child to obtain many sons.
One should draw a hexagon, then a circle, and thereafter draw an eight-petaled lotus;
O Supreme Goddess, one should also write the six long vowels within the hexagons.
Then one should write "aiṃ hrīṃ oṃ aiṃ hrīṃ phaṭ svāhā" upon the eight petals;
thereafter, O Goddess, one should write it in the very center—listen to this, O Maheśvarī! (19)

Then, having written the Praṇava, followed by Māyā, and the name of the practitioner in the dative case (ṅe-anta), and having written "suputraṃ" (a good son), one should then utter the word "utpādaya" (beget). || 20 ||
Having thus prepared it according to the rules, one should wear this supreme yantra;
O Goddess, by wearing it, all prosperity shall be attained—of this there is no doubt.
Worship has been explained previously. One should worship the Goddess with the Kālī-mantra.
O beloved of my life, listen now to the subjugation [rite] and the subjugation yantra.
O beloved, by the mere retention of which one may again bring others under one's control.
Having drawn a square with four corners, one should then draw an eight-petaled lotus; on each petal, one should write: "Oṃ, bind the mouth of the enemy! (oṃ śatrumukhaṃ bandhaya).
Having inscribed his name and worn it upon his arm, O Auspicious One,
one should worship the Goddess as before and recite her mantra one hundred thousand times according to the prescribed rule.
O Goddess, the practitioner should worship according to the ritual prescribed for Cāmuṇḍā; and by performing the fire-oblation according to the rule, he certainly becomes a master over all. (25)
First, one should draw the Bandhamuktayantra; outside that, one should write the vowels; having drawn two circles on the outside, one should write "hrīṃ" in the four directions.
One should draw a lotus with two rows of petals and eight petals using yellow orpiment or similar substances;
by wearing it on the neck, the region of the throat, or even on the crest-lock, [one attains the desired result].
Likewise, his liberation from bondage shall occur on the ninth day;
the wise man should then recite the Durgā mantra one hundred thousand times according to the previously mentioned procedure.

One should draw two circles there, containing the four great seed-syllables, as a yantra for destroying the fear of ḍākinīs and the like, and as a yantra for ensuring that one’s children live; having drawn two squares on the outside, if one wears it [as an amulet], [the purpose is achieved]. (29)

It destroys in a mere instant the fear arising from ḍākinīs and other such spirits. If a woman who has given birth to stillborn children becomes overwhelmed by grief, she should wear this supreme yantra; thereupon, her children will come to life.
Having drawn two long lines, one should draw an eight-petaled lotus upon that body;
O Śivā, one should write "Oṃ Hrīṃ Devadatta Hrīṃ" in the middle of the lines.
On the petal at the beginning of the line, one should write "Oṃ Hūṃ," and on the petal at the end of the line, "Oṃ";
using either yellow orpiment and saffron, or likewise with lac.
O Supreme Goddess, O Queen of Gods, she whose name is written and placed within the five nectars (pañcāmṛta) shall indeed become one whose offspring are living.
O beloved Śivā, for his son, untimely death shall not occur otherwise;
likewise, O Śivā, one should perform worship in the manner described and recite the mantra one hundred thousand times.
[Thus ends the twentieth chapter in the Kriyoḍḍīśa, the Great King of Tantras, in the dialogue between the Goddess and the Lord. || 20 ||

Vijayā as an adjunct; Vijayā, when combined with milk, is traditionally held to bestow great splendor.
Because it causes the agitation and purification of the elements, it removes the defects of the eyes.
Taken with water, it indeed destroys diseases such as indigestion in an instant;
taken with ghee, it generates intelligence, bestows the goddess of speech, and brings others under one's control.
It destroys all disorders of the phlegm (kapha) without exception when taken with honey;
indeed, combined with rock salt, it increases the digestive fire (jaṭharāgni). || 3 ||
When consumed together with sugar, salt, and jaggery,
it destroys sour bile (amlapitta) as well as colic pain at that very moment.
She is said to bestow the nourishment of fruits, to produce sweet sounds, to grant the knowledge of liberation (kaivalya), and thus to be the giver of all perfections (siddhis). || 5 ||
